articles.text:
MIXED TRIBUNALS FOR TRADE
OFFENCES.

WIT r.r. working men throughout the country
during the last year were crying out against
the perfidious ambiguities of the Criminal Law
Amendment Act, they little thought that
they were altogether on a false scent, and that
their employers could afford to make thern a
present of that measure in any shape they
might prefer to have it. It haajr‘eii clearly
shown by Mr. Justice Bum that two or more
men respectfully declining to continue working
unless their employer complies with their con-
ditions can be sentenced to twelve months'
imprisonment with hard labour for 'conspir-
ing to coerce" him, which is an offence at
common law, and is likely to remain so, let
the. language of the Criminal Law Amend-
ment Act be what it will.
According V) the Times report of the Gas
Stokers' trial, "the prinoipal count in the in-
dictment accused them of conspiring together
to injure, prejudice, and annoy the company,
and to endeavour to force them to make altera- ,
tions in their mode of business. The prisoners
were especially charged with conspiring by
threats and menaces to extort from Mr.
TREWDY, the Superintendent of the Company,
a promise, contrary to his own free will, to re-
instate the prisoner DILLY in the service of
the company, to the damage of the company,
and in restraint of trade and the freedom of
action; and Mr. Justice BRETT, in his sum-
ming up, said "There would be improper
molestation if there was anything done to
cause annoyance, or in the way of unjustifiable
interference, which, in the judgment of the
jury, would have the effect of annoying or
interfering with the minds of ordinary persons
carrying on such a business as that of a gas
company." According to the Spectator this
"amounts to a decision, that to lead an agita-
tion for a strike is a highly penal offence, Mr.
Justice BRETT expressly stating that the
failure to give notice was not of the essence of
the crime." •

Since the last Reform Bill the power of
Inaking, repealing, and amending the laws
has lain 'with the working classes—if they
choose to bestir themselves. It may be ex-
pected that at the impending general election
they will be more disposed to use this power
than they were at the last, and that they will
want their legal advisers to inform them how
they may use it in such a way as to take thi
tremendous weapon out of the bands of their
emplgers.
I doubt whether their legal adiiisers will be
able to give them any satisfactory answer. It
may not be easy to say how the law of con-
spiracy—which, STRAIGIIT, said, "is

one of the most elastic offences known to the
criminal law "—can be limited sufficiently to
protect workmen against the prejudices of
middle-class judges and juries, without at the
same time 'giving impunity to many crimes of
the worst sort. We cannot have such a law
without leaving much to the discretion of
judges and juries; and we shall not be far
wrong if we affirm more broadly and ge,aerally,
that as long as the administration of justice is
placed exclusively in the hands of the middle
and upper classes, means will always be found
to make any law bear hardly on. workmen in
all disputes with their employers, however
carefully it may have been worded with a View
to prevent such oppression.
When the agitation for the amendment of
the laws affecting trades unions Was com-
menced in 1867, I urged the Conference of
Amalgamated Trades to introduce into their
Bill a clause providing that juries in all trials
under the proposed Act should be taken by
ballot from the Electoral Registrar in order
that they might have a chance of containing
a fair proportion of working men. All .who
were present at the meetingaof that Conference
will remember how pertinaciously I argued for
the adoption of mY suggestion. The first Bill
prepared did contain such a clause, but it dis-
appeared when members of Parliament took
it in hand. lam now more firmly convinced
than over that until this or some equivalent
guarantee for fair dealing is accorded to work-
men, all other legislation will be practically
useless.

it may be objected that the plan of mixed
juries would break down from the difficulty of
withdrawing workmen from their employment,
at short notice; to serve on juries. But I have
no doubt that this difficulty might be very
easily overcome if there was a serious bona
fide desire to meet it. A more valid objection
may be made from the workman's point of
view. When we see Mr. Justice BRETT dis-
regarding the recommendation to mercy of
even his middle-class jury, and inflicting a
savagely end punishment, we are driven to
ask whether 'workmen must not have some
voice, not only in giving verdicts, but in pro-
nouncing sentences. There has .been a good
deal of talk lately about giving legal sanction
to the decisions of councils of arbitration
composed equally of employers and em-
ployed. I rather, think there has been a
Bill for that purpose before Parliament.
If such tribunals can be constituted legally
for one purpose they can for another; RUCI I
would put it to workmen whether, consider-
ing the hopelessness of obtaining justice from
existing tribunals, they should not insist that
all eases coming under the head of trade dis-
putes should be withdrawn from the j uriediction
of ordinary courts, and decided by tribunals,
constituted after the pattern of councils of
arbitration, that is to
,say, consisting of em-
ployers and employed in equal numbers, and
invested with the power to inflict such penal-
ties as the laws in their pruent or amended
state may provide.
- -

No doubt such a proposal as this will seem
little short of blasphemous to the middle and
upi er classes, and their organs, the lawyers.
But that is no reason whatever why it Echould
not be considered carefully by woilcmen, and,
if it meets their approval, put into execution
by the powers which the last Reform Bill
vested in their hands. We arc in the midst of
a social and industrial revolution, and if the

Summonses got out against them by the
bushel. At one court five hundged in a batch.
They are hunted like wild and dangerous
cattle; driven into court after court, and sent
from those places into gaol as felons with a be-
wildering rapidity. Those committed for trial
at the Old Bailey were, like all the rest, poor
men—men unused to deal in any way with the
law. Charged with a common offence, they had
no time, they had no power to consult amongst
themselves or with their friends as to what was
best to be done. The solicitors employed on
their behalf had to fight their way over official
obstructions into their cells to consult with
them. There was no time to prepare a defence,
no fair opportunity of getting together woes,
sary evidence, no time for defending counsel to
study their briefs. Under such circumstances
it was of the very essence of justice that the
trials should have been postponed. No inte-
rest could have suffered by it, no individual
injury could have arisen. Even the most pre-
judiced could not have condemned such a pro-
ceeding. In a few weeks time, if the men
were guilty, the law could have been as tho-
roughly vindicated as it has been, without the
outrage against justice and propriety which
has taken place as the matter stands.

Then again, it may be asked, wilat good end
is served by such legal vengeance Does it re-
quire crowds of victims to prove to men they
have made a blunder which even in their own
interest they evict never think of repeating ?
These Men had only just commenced the orga-
nization of their union. They acted precipi-
'lately and without advice. No friend of
unionism could or would approve their conduct,
and to say 'nothing of any other punishment,
the loss of their employment would have been
a lesson to them of very great severity. But
if the law must be vindicated, surely it Was
neither wise nor humane to vindicate it in a
manner which cannot but ho injurious to
society. If men break the law their punish-
ment should not ho such as to amount to actual
porsonalquin. A number of these gas stokers
who have been summarily convicted may when,
they come out not find their homes actually
broken up, and their wives and children in
the workhouse ; but many of them may ; and
what advantage there can be to have a number
of persons thrown perhaps perpanently us
paupers on the rates, we leave the friends of
legal vengeance to find out. Certainly, th
how's of the men who have got twelvemonths
each, unless extraneous aid be brought to
them, must become desolate—their wives made
wretched, their children left without shelter or
food, Again we ask, who gains by this ?
where does the profit arise ?

The law is not vindicated, It is no
vindication Of law to administer it amidst grave
doubts, in oven impartial inen's minds, as to
its justice," with certain Convictions, in the
minds of many, as to its inhumanity. The
JUDGE declared, in passing senteneo, that the
" time had come " ttauth men, in union a
lesson, and certainly in doing this justice
Bur rr did rise fully to the Iwight Of an
enraged schoolmaster of tho most ferocious
type. His legal eat had wire in the
strings, like those used in jimmies,
was Meant to lacerate and it Las done se.
-But if the Junon had a lesson to touch, the
werking Men of Great Britain have one to
earn. They will had ant by this verdict and
exitance that any act .they do celled' cely may
be eel-tits-W(1 and punished as conspiracy, and

We have beenassured that Justice IinETT is a

If, however, these preliminary lessons have the

had law w.iieli can be pressed against them,

anyone to their injury, They have the power,
and they must use it, if they intend to strike
down those -degrading and disabling laws
which exolude them from the high ground
of an independent citizenship. This case, in
all its requirements, must be properly treated

LLOYD JONES.

TIIE IMPRISONED OAS STOKERS.

IN my opinion the sentence on the gas
stokers is oppressive and vindictive. 1 have
already said that I regard the strike as wrong
and unjustifiable, and that the men who had
broken their contracts were punishable under.
the Masters and Servants Act. But the actual
sentence inflicted was net under that Act, nor
under the Criminal Law Amendment Act,
the maximum penalty of bAli Acts being
three 'Mouths' imprisonment.
As a lawyer I am bound to accept the
decision of the judge es to the effect of the
law of conspiracy, novel as that decision is in
such a case as this; but as a citizen I repeat
my opinion that the sentence was oppressive
and vindictive. It is plain that the freedom
of every unionist, end indeed of every work-
man in the country, is at the mercy of a judge
acting under the irritation of public feeling.
1 consider it the first duty of every work-
man to put this question now before every
other political question whatever, and to
agitatO in every lawful way for a complete re-

vision of all the laws affecting. workmen,
The middle classes are breaking contracts
every, day, and.. inducing ca--4h other to break

cloacae§ for their own ends, as the litigation

in civil courts prove. But it would bc looked
• upon as monstrous that a trader should be
sent to prison for breaking a contract in con-
cert with others. Workmen who concert to
break a contract are sent to prison for 12
months. And' even, as in DILLY'S case, who
broke no contract, those who are parties to
any combined movement which involves a

_
breach of contract are liable to the same im-
prisonment. I nerd hardly point out that
every person throughout the kingdom who
can he shown to have taken part in a strike
where any breach of contract arises, and under
the Bystem of yearly Wrings every labourers'
strike has more or less of this character, may
be made liable under this new application of
the
.doctrine of conspiracy, to 12 or more
months' imprisonment, at the option of a judge.
And the judge's words go even further than
this,

I use sw-,11 language under the gravest sense
of responsibility ; but I give it as my deliberate

opinion that. there is effect, if not in words,
one law for the rich and one for the poor at
this moment in England.
I consider it the first duty of working men
to reform this injustice, and till it is done, I
look upon political questions as idle. A. Liberal
Government under which a State Of things
like this can be consolidated, is, in my opinion,
rnoclizery.

2. That the matter should be brought'before
Parliament. ,

3. A national agitation" for the complete
revision of all the penal legislation affecting
workmen.

2. The Criminal Law Amendment Act.

As the law now stands in the irritation of the
employing class, of successful strikes, and the
readiness of judges to lend themselves to this
irritation, I hold that no working man is safe.

THE CONVICTION FOR CONSPIRACY
WOIMING LEN must not suppose ,that the
conviction of the gas stokers for censpiracy
was illkgal or.against the law. There should
be no misunderstanding onthis point. That is
not the grievance of which they have to cm-
plain, or the . danger which lies before-thew.
The conviction was perfectly legal. There is
no doubt about it. Whenever two or more.
,persons agree or combine together to commit a
crime, or to induce anybody to commit a
.crirno, that .is a conspiracy at; common • law.
One of the charges against the gas stokers was
that they. • combined toget4er to commit an
offence against the Masters and Servants 'Act. •
The judge was only doing his.duty in telling'
the jury that this constituted the crime Of.
conspiracy. The whole fault lies in the exist-.
once of an Act Of 'Parliament, the Masters and
Servants Act, which makes breach of contract'
'crime. Bat there is a, ranch more serious'
'danger to workmen than either this or the ex-
cessive punishment meted out by the court in
this particular ease. The judge, in explaining
the law of conspiracy to the jury,- used ex-
pressions and definitions of the most unex-
pected kind ; the effect of which is to render
the position of trades societies and Combina-
tions Of 'workmen 'extremely dangerous. .V 0
words used in defining conspiracy by Mr. Jus-
tice MEW, will include, if not every strike,'
almost every strike that can be undertaken.
And if men are ever resolved to strike, they will
have to do so at the peril of being tried and
convicted of conspiracy:
There are two courses now to be adopted ;
firstly, to get all the penal laws affecting
workmen, specially, repealed; secondly, to
support tho-werkmen's defence committee. I
again urge the trades societies to support the
committee liberally. Every case of conspiracy.
must be fought. I.have a very strong' belief
that the law as laid down by Mr. Justice
,BEETT is untenable, and the sooner it can be
tested the better. Therefore, trades societies,
should give the committee power and authority
to act in their names ; that is to say, they
should send in their sanction to the committee,
that the defence of any man charged with
conspiracy should be undertaken in the name
of all the trade societies of the United
ICing-
dom. The liberties of the working classes have
never been more seriously threatened.., Work-
men ought not to rest until these crushing laws
are repealed. Effort and agitation is the
solemn duty of everr workman who has any
feeling of self-respect or any desire for hide-.
pendence and freedom.

PR,UGEESS AND CHIIISTLINITY.

WELL -IN*RUOTED Christians ougnt to
welcome any illustrations, such as Mr. HENRY
CROMPTON proposes to give in your columns,
of human progress. We are taught to look
forward to a day when, by pursuing truth in
love, we may arriveithrough a perfect organi-
zation and adjustment of parts unto a fully
developed humanity (Ephesians . iv. 12-16).
The Christian, because he believes that
"through the ages one increasing purpose
runs," is pledged to believe in a progress which
has Or its end the perfection of mankind.
The "n4vw earth wherein dwells righteousness'
is an appointed object of Christian aspiration.
Eight*ousness, or social order, is a perpetual
burden of Bible prophecy.
, I admit that this hope has been far too little
encouraged. by popular
.Christian doctrine ;
but it might he illustrated out of every great
and authoritative Christian writer from Sr.
PATTI., downwards, And it is by its best
teaching, and not by its worst—as we all need
to be reminded—that any system ought to be
judged. For .this reason I deprecate the
selection of such examples of Christian teach-
ing as those which are given by Mr. HENRY
CROMPTON. They might he proved by quota-
tions, to have been put forward by Chris-
taus, but they are not characteristic Christian j
doctrines. Our most reasonable appeal is to
the Founder of Western Christianity, Sr.
PAUL ; and inhim, not to Casual remarks, but
to his leading convictions. First, as to the
relation of Woman to man. I certainly believe„
there is truth in the story which connects
man's entrance into conscious shame with the
influence of woman upon him. But the express
Christian doctrine is that "the woman is the
glory of the man ;" that," neither is the man
without the woman, neither the woman with-
out the man, in the LORD ", (I. Corinthians xi.
7-11). Similarly as to the meaning of labour.
There aro two aspects of it. It surely has
been, and is, a curse. But the Christian doc-
trine condemns idleness absolutely in all—(1I. •
The. iii. 11, 12)—and teaches men to labour
unweariedly in hope, "always abounding in the
work of the LOUD,. knowing that their labour
is not in vain in the LOUD" (I. Cor. kv. 'SS).
The third example, the statement that "man
on this earth is a stranger and a sojourner '
in a foreign . land," is connected with' a pro-
founder paradox, like that which affirms that
a man, to save himself, rnust lose himself.
Unquestionably, the New Testament—not the
Old—teaches that man's true. citizenship is in
an invisible realm; and I am willing to adtnq
that this doctrine, being perverted, has some-
times " withdrawn men's attention and efforts
too much from their true sphere of. work."
But I do not think it fits ever been what Mr.
HENRY CROMPTON calls it, "deadly and. para-
lyzing." As a general rule I believe it to be
demonstrable that the belief in another world
has been the most powerful inspiration for
'useful work in this world. I appeal' again to
St. PAni., not as a teacher, but as an example.
Who will allege that he was paralyzed by his
faith? What intelligent critic will refuse him
credit for having given a remarkable impulse
to social progress?

articles.text:
THE NEW KNOWLEDGE

IN the three papers on "Education for the
New System" (in the BEE-HIVE of November
9th and 16th, and of December 7th), I have
pointed out that it is necessary before the
only social reform which can be effectual can
be realised, that those who are to be the lead-
ing agents in initiating it should acquire
what may be called a new intellectual and

moral character. I :have pointed out that,
intellectually, they must acquire new know-
ledge; knowledge of which mankind have ,
hitherto been ignorant; the knowledge of the
causes, beginning with the primary causes, of
evil and of geed in the formation of character ;
and that morally they must acquire the
enlightened goodness, or the right develop-
ment of their mqral nature, which cannot
exist in man while he is ignorant, as all have
hitherto been, of the causes of evil and of
good. Let the reader ask himself whether he
knows, or whether he is acquainted with any-
one who knows, these causes. " No," he I‘ill
be obliged to say, "I do not." Of course ho
does not; unless he, or his acquaintance, has
read very attentively, and has studied, what
I have written upon the subject. Does it then
appear to him to be worth his while to take a
little trouble to acquire new knowledge which
it is obvious must bo of such incalculable
importance? 'lf it does not, ho must remain
in ignorance .of the subject; and any opinion
which he may form upon it must be worthless.
And any remarks which he may make Iwo
the subject of social reform must be worthless.
And anything which he can do for the prit-
motion of social reform must be of very little
value. For what can anyone know about
social reform who is ignorant of the causes of
evil and of good to man?
But to get the new knowledge is only to
acquire a part, the intellectual part, of the new
character. The social reformer must also
acquire to some extent the other, the mOl5l,
part of it, before be can understand the subject.
The man can have but little claim to be °ldled
a social reformer who has not conquered in
himself the irascibility, the bitterness, the
petty spitefulness, the malevolence, the in-
tolerance, the vindictiveness, towards those
who displease him, which are tho °Nato of
ignorance and erroneous ideas in reference to
the causes of evil- and of good, and which

articles.title: PROGRESS. No. 111.
articles.text:
PROGRESS.
No. 111.

IN writing these articles upon pi!ogross, I
would not have anybody suppose
_thatl am
pretending to give an exhaustive treatment of
so vast a subject.. That eonldunly-be done by
a ystematio. exposition of the whole of social
science, of the 'laws of the existence and move-
ment of: humanity: My sole• object is to
awaken the interest of thoughtftil -men, and
show them that whatever difficulties there may
be, whatever gaps that 'require to be filled up,'
the positive -or scientific Method has invaded
an 4. taken possession of the field of human
,
thought,, constituting and building ,up . a
body of knowledge, which explain the
phenomena of the . external world and of
humanity, in the only way in which they can
be explained, namely, by reference to their
laws, and which affords to man in his weakness
a provision capable of guiding and directing
human life. The constructive phase of social
life has begun already, pushing out the destruc-
tive and the chimerical. A gradual substitution
has • been taking place, of certainty and
experience for the fancies. and guesswork by
which men heretofore have been content to be,

guided.
The first condition of progress is, as I bay°
shown, the fact of tho fixity of the natural
order, in other words, the invariability of the
highest laws. The second condition is that
phenomena arc capable of being modified;
and when we possess scientific knowledge they
admit of systematic modification. 1 come now
to the fundamental idea of law. The progress
of which I write is progress according to law.
All the various processes involved in the term
progress, such as the movement onwards of
humanity, its growth, its organisation and
development, are subordinate to, and take
place by, virtue of laws. What is a law? A
law is an abstract fact, expressing a relation
between other facts, which are less general.
It is an expression of the way or mode in
which events occur. , When a ray of light is
thrown upon a mirror, • it is reflected in a
definite way; the laws which govern the
reflection or light, include all cases of reflected
light, and express the mode in which light is
reflected, and it cannot be otherwise when
light passes through a substance, it does so
according to laws of refraction. These laws
are beyond man's power to alter, but they do
not prevent his interference with the pheno-
mena of light. On the contrary, by knowledge
of the laws of light, he has been able to con-
struct such things as the telescope and the
microscope, thereby increasing man's power
and giving him insight into worlds, which,
-therwise, would have remaine4 outside the

sphere of human knowledge. I might multiply
examples to show that our power has been
gained over events only, because the mode of
their occurrence is fixed, and, not arbitrary.
I may mention, byway of example, such in-
ventions as the thermometer, barometer,
steam-engine, Sea., all of which depend on the
existence of invariable laws. But this, Which
is not denied . in mathematics, in physical
science, in oliemistry, or even in the science
of,life, is denied by some persons to be appli-
cable to social life and morals. Now every
great advance that. has been made in science
has been obstinately denied. GALILEO'S
'scientific dernonstration of the double move-
ment of the earth was denied, because it up-
set the religious explanation of the external
world, which Was at that time generally be-
lieved in, and showed that so far from
man and, the earth being the centre of
the universe round which all things moved,
the earth was, on the contrary, not even the
centre of its own system, but was only a small
fragment in a universe, too vast f)r man to
c meeive, much less to measure, liVe_seo in our
own day the absurd and bigoted attacks upon
Mr, DARWIN. Whatever speculative differences
there may be among thinking men, it is now
a truth aocepted by all the best intellects in
Europe, that the principle of law is universal;
that all phenomena of whatsoever kind are
subordinate to law; that scientific methods arc
the only possible means of arriving at truth.
This was first enunciated as a general proposi-
tion by the famous Frenchman MoNTESQIITETT,
in his great book, "The Spirit of Laws," and
since then it has become a recognised and
accepted doctrine, capable of resisting all the
assaults of criticism or misrepresentation.
iLecoN's saying, "Knowledge is power." is
strictly true. Positive science is the only basis
and means of systematic notion; action not
merely to modify the external woild, but to
regulate and develop our inner nature. What
I have said wilt indicate the absurdity of the
talk of some of our manufacturers and politi-
cians, who, being grossly ignorant of every-
thing like a scientific conception, palm off with
magnificent flourishes, all sorts of stuff about
the laws of political economy, and preach a
childish creed of laissez-faire or do nothing,"
saying, that we cannot modify the facts of
industry, because industrial phenomena are '
subordinate to, laws. On the contrary; it is
precisely hes:muse there are stroll laws that we
can modify the industrial world. In fact,
men found out by experience, ages and ages
before they understood the reason, that such
modifications were practic 11. Hence our at-
tempts at political and sodial improvement,
which have gone on at first blindly and
instinctively; but by degrees, as knowledge
advanced, those attempts were made with
,
greaterforesiht and prudence. It has been
so in every branch of human life. The pro-
giess of humanity has been spontaneous, in-
stinetive, and unconscious, like the life of a
child. But when a certain stage of progress
has been revelled, men became conscious of the
movement that was going on, and the human
intellect was impelled to discover the laws
of that progress. That has been ac-
complished. Henceforth, progress can only
be conscious, intentilnal, and systematic ;
worked out by organised effort, based upon
the knowledge of the laws of social
science. There can be no reversion or turning
back. We cannot now progress unconsciously
and without system. Social forces have been
developed of prodigious strength, which
rightly used and directed are the means of
advance, but which if untrained and without
restraint or guidance only tend to clash and
produce discord. These forces are capable of
a good use or a bad use. The true conception
of the life and progress of humanity, is that of
the convergence of all forces and all indivi-
duals by conscious effort towards perfection.
That is the true religion, and GobITE says,
that as there can be but one health, so there
can be but ono religion. Science is the de-
monstrated doctrine of that religion.

We want to know then with respect to the
progress of humanity, of what it consists, and
the manner in which it takes part. One great
fact, obtained from the whole of 'science, that
is, from the whole experience of mankind, is that
this progress has been accomplished by a

articles.title: BEE-HIVE.
articles.text:
THE BEE-HIVE.

gradual process of development, and not by
sudden jumps, leaps, or creations. We cannot
follow every step in the process ; we cannot
reach back to the origin of all things; we can-
not solve the question of the final purpose of
all that we see around us. The beginning and
the end, the, origin and the purpose, the first
cause and the final cause, are problems far
beyond the capacity and power of the human
race ; but we can know bow this development
has taken place, the mode in which it has
come to pass, that is to say, its laws. If, for
example, we turn again to those phenomena
over which man's intellect has accomplished
a most triumphant success, to that science,
which human genius has reduced most perfect,
astronotny,—we find that although the astrono-
mical phenomena have been 'reduced, to the
greatest simplicity by their being referred to
and grouped under that famous generalization,
the law of gravity; yet, notwithstanding, we
knew no more as to the or origin as to the
final purpose of these events, than we
did before the days of NEWTON. The
Path of knowledge is the path of science; all
others lead astray, to futile. efforts and to
wasted life.

I shall in my next article soy something
with respect to the development of humanity,
or its progress, as a whole. After that I shall
proCeed to the consideration of the diffaent
kinds of progress.

HENRY CROMPTON.
(To be continued.) "

articles.text:
THE' TRIAL.

Lust week we inserted a. summary of the trial
of the 4as-stokeril and their sentences. We now
give the Summing up' of the judge and his chlrge
to the jury:—

Mr. Justice Prat, in summing up the case,
told the jury the defendants were charged with
having entered into a criminal conspiraCy. It
had been stated that the results of that con-
spiracy might, have be ii, if not otherwise. Pre-
vented, supposing it existed,,
,most lamentable to
the public it had been Said on the other Side that
even though that might have been so, the j urr
ought not to allow themselves, in finding a verdict,
to be influenced by any such considerations. lie,
entirely agreed with the latter part of that observa-
tion. They meat not allow themselves to be
influenced by the view that if there was an agree-
ment among the defendants to cease work it might
have .had a lamentable effect on this ' city. He
entirely agreed that, so far as the defendants were
the servants of the gas company, they had no
obligation whatever in regard to the public. They
had entered into .no. agreenient with the public;
the public paid them nothieg for their labour.
Tho,. question the jury would have to determine
was whether as servants of the gas company they
had, or some of them had, been guilty of a criminal
conspiracy. The definition Of conspiracy gene-
rally was, this: if people agreed together
t.) do so, some unlawfulyfing and proceeded to do
it they were guilty of conspiracy. They would
have to consider whether the defendants, or two of
them or more, had agreed together to do an un-
lawful net; or to de a lawful act by unlawful
means. They could not find one man Only guilty
of conspiracy, but where they. had live men they
were not bound to find them all guilty. They
might make a distinction between them. He
should first ask thorn this—Was there an agree-
ment or combination between the • defendants,.
either or some of them, to force Alr. Trewby or the .
company to conduct the business of the company
contrary to their will by an improper threat or im-
proper molestation. There would be improper
molestation if there was anything done to cause
annoyance or in the way of unjustifiable inter-
ference, which, in the judgment of the jury would
have the effect of annoying or interfering with the
minds.of ordinary persona carrying on such 'a busi-
ness as that of a gas company. It was enough if
they thought there was molestation intended and
agreed upon with an improper intent which in
their judgment would be an annoyance and an
unjustifiable' interference with the business and
have a deterring effect on the minds of air. Tn.*.
by and the company. The mere fact of those men
being members of a trade union was not illegal,
nor ought it to be pressed against thorn. The
mere circumstance of their leaving their work and
breaking their contracts was not a sufficient ground
for the jury finding thorn guilty under this indiet
meat; but if there was an agreement by molestation
to control the members of the company, he said
that was a conspiracy,at common law, and such an
offence was not abrogated by the Criminal Lave
Amendment Act, which had been quoted: Con-
spiraey, however, was charged in another form—
namely, that they either agreed to do in unlawful
act or to do a lawful act by unlawful means; and
ho asked the jury Whether there was a combinatien
between the defendants either to binder or prevent
the company from carrying on their business by
means of the men simultaneously breaking the
contract of service they had entered into with the
company. It was au illegal act, and—what was
more—a criminal act. If they did agree to inter-
fere with their employers' business by simul-
taneously breaking such contracts they were then
agreeing to do that which would bring them within
the definition of conspiracy.

The jury retired, and, after being absent about
20 minutes, returned into court with a verdict of
Guilty against all the defend Ants, accompanied by
a strong recommendation to mercy on account of
their great ignorance, of their having been misled,
and of their previous good character.
Mr. Justice Brett, in passing sentence, said ho
was sorry to see men of their character convicted
of a criminal offence ; but to his mind the evidence
was so convincing that the jury could do nothing
but convict them. It; was now his duty, and
upon hint rested the responsibility, of coming to
a °lnclusion as to the kind of offence which they
had committed. They had been convicted of a
conspiracy, and if he thought that conspiracy was
a light one, or that there wore extenwiting air
.ctunstanees with regard to their conduct, although
s
the conspiracy was not a light one, he hould be
bound to pass on them a light sentence; but if be
came to the conclusion that the conspiracy was a
bad one, and if he could not SOO any extenuating
circumstances in regard to their conduct, he VMS

4

bound to pass a severe sentence. That seemed
to him to be the law, and the rule of conduct that
was binding ;von him as the administrator of the
law in passing sentence. He had told the jury
that on the question whether they were to find
them guilty or not they ought not to be influenced
by the suggestion that what they were attempting
to do would be dangerous to the public. But it
did seem to him now, when he was called on to
consider what kind of conspiracy they had been

guilty, of that be could nct throw aside what was
one of the obvious results of the conspiracy into
which they entered, and what must have been in
their minds; and be could not doubt that the
obvious result was great danger to the public of
this metropolis; that that danger was present to
their minds; and it was by the acting on that
knowledge and on the effect they thought it would
have upon their masters' minds, and trading
upon their knowledge of the danger, that they
entered into this conspiracy in order to force their
masters to follow their will. It was true
they wore men of good character before. That
made him sorry they were convicted of a crime
at all ; but ho could not think in this particular
case of conspiracy he could share the opinion that
they were misled or that
.they were ignorant. It
seemed to him that it was just that good character
that had put it into their power to mislead others.
The jury had said that in their opinion they were
misled. If it had been necessary that those facts
should be decided in order to arrive at a verdict,
the judgment and the accuracy of that opinion
would have been entirely with the jury, and it
would have been beyond his province to interfere
with it, and the jury would have been masters
of their decision; but when it came by way of re-
commendation by the jury it was a matter on
which be was sorry to say he must form his
opinion, and, notwithstanding the great deference
ho was in the habit of paying to the recommenda-
tions of juries, he ,was sorry on this occasion not
only to say he disagreed with them as to the
prisoners' ignorance, but he could see no trace of
evidence to justify any man in coming to such a
conclusion. He saw no proof of their ignorance.
On the contrary, there was the way in which they
carried out the matter, and the design itself being

formed with such accuracy as to what must be the
obvious result of what they were about to do,
and the effect it would have upon their masters.
The very design of the conspiracy showed that,
so far fr9ra being ignorant men, they were men of
very considerable intelligence, or they could not
have designed or carried out such a conspiracy.
As to their being misled, he knew not against
whom the suggestion was made. lie confessed he
could not see any man who might be fairly
said to have misled them. There was a man who
ought to have been by their side, but whether
he was more guilty it was not for him to
say. Ile referred to the man Webbe. That
man was not there; he ought to have been there.
So far from agreeing with the jury that they
were misled, it seemed to him that, from the course
, they took during the whole of these proceedings,
they were not the men misled, but the men mis-
leading, and that it was they who misled the
others, and most of the 500 obeyed what they had
suggested. The prisoners were the principals—
the chief actors; two of them were delegates chosen
by the men, and therefore evidently men to whom
they looked up. They took a leading part in the
conspiracy. Therefore, notwithstanding their good
character they had unfortunately put themselves
into the position of being properly convicted of a
dangerous and wicked conspiracy. The time had
come when a serious Punishment and not w nominal
or a light one must be inflicted—a punishment that
would teach men in their position that although
without off( Imo they might be members of a trade
union or might agree to go into an employment
or to leave it without committing any offence, yet
that they must take elre when they agreed
together that they must not agree to do it by illegal
means. If they did that they were guilty of
conspiracy, and if they mislead others they were
guilty of a wicked conspiracy. The sentence he
had to pass on them was that they' be kept in prison
for 12 calendar months.

FOILMATION OF COMMITTEE.

A special meeting of the Committee, which was
formed on Monday, the 16th inst., for defending
the five gas stokers indicted, tried, aucl convicted
id the Ohl Bailey, last week, was held on Saturday
afternoon last at Bolt-court, Fleet-street, Mr.
'George Potter in the chair. Amongst those pre-
sent were Mr. W. Allan, engineers; Mr. D. Guiles,
iroefounders ; Mr. G. Potter, joiners; Mr. IL
Broadhurst, stonenntoons ; Mr. llowell, Secretary
Parliamentary Committee Trades Congress; Mr.
R. M. Latham, President Labour Representation
League; Mr. T. Mottersith id, silk weavers; Mr.
R. Applegatth, earpenters ; Mr. Sinclair, General
Union of Carpenteta ; Mr, Ryan, Labour Leap();

Mr. T. G. Facey, painters; Mr. T. Hughes, M.P. ;
Mr. W. Cobbett ; and Mr. W. Mackenzie. The
following gentlemen were represented by letters :
Captain Maas°, Mr. F. Harrison, Mr. H. Cromp-
ton, Professor Beesly, and Mr. Ashton, Rope-
makers' Society.
The chairman said the above meeting was con-
vened for the purpose of considering the best
means to be adopted to obtain redress for the fol-
lowing men :—Messrs. Dilley, Rey, Bunn, Wilson,
and Jones, being gas stokers convicted and sen-
tenced at the Old Bailey on Thursday, December
19th, on a charge of conspiracy. The principal
object of the meeting was to ascertain really under
what law the men had been convicted and the
best means to be adopted for obtaining a remis-
sion of the monstrous sentences both at the Old
Bailey and the police-courts. Letters throwing
some light upon the question had been received
from Messrs. Sheen and Roscoe, the solicitors who
had conducted the defence at the Old Bailey, and
from other members of the cothmittee, unable to
attend that day.

Mr. H. Broadhurst,. secretary, then read the
above letters, of which the following are the lead-
ing points :—Messrs. Sham and Roscoe say "The
jury convicted the prisoners upon the third count
of the indictment, whieh charged them with con-
spiring to break their contracts with the company
by leaving thti company's service without giving
the notice required by the contracts they had
entered into. . . . The law, as laid down by
Mr. Justice Brett, is so wide that, if it were held
to be good law, it would be very difficult for any
body of men to combine together to obtain terms
from their employers which the employers might
not be ready to grant of their own free will, with-
out exposing themselves to the risk of a criminal
prosecution for conspiracy."

Mr. Crompton says
"I think that the conviction was strictly legal,
on the ground that every combination to commit
a crime is a conspiracy in point of law, and
the conviction was on the count of the
indictment charging a conspiracy to commit a
crime against the Masters and Servants Act. At
the same time, the summing up by Mr. justice
Brett—and especially his views respecting molesta-
tion—are of the most dangerous character. They
would cover and include every strike, and under
such a law no workman is safe tor ,a moment."
Mr. F. Hat rison says: "In my opinion the sentence
on them, as stokers, is oppressive and vindictive.

I regard the strike as wrong and unjustifiable, and
the men who had broken their contracts were
punishable under the Masters and Servants Act.
But the sentence inflicted, was not under that
Act, nor under the Criminal Law Amendment
Act, the maximum penalty of both acts being
three months' imprisonment. . . . It is

plain that the freedom of every trades' unionist,
and, indeed, of every workman in the country, is
at the mercy of a judge acting under the irritation
of public feeling. . . Every person throughout
the kingdom who can be shown to have taken
part in a strike where any breach of contract arises,
and, under the system of yearly hirings, every
labourer's strike has heen more or less of this
character, may be mode liable, under this new
application of the doctrine of conspiracy, to twelve
or more months' imprisonment, at the option of a
judge. And the judge's words go even further than
this,"

Professor Beesly wrote :—" They certainly be-
haved foolishly and wrongly, but the. ticattnent
they aro receiving from magistrates and judges is
simply atrocious, and it is the interest as well as
the duty of all trades unionists to take the matter
up with the utmost energy. But resolutions and
meetings are of no use unless followed by action—
you must bring pressure to boar on Gladstone and
Bruce, and on borough members everywhere. If
these will not do what you want, that is, get the
men released and the law altered, you must have
them all out at the next election."

Considerable discussion followed the reading of
the above letters, general surprise being expressed
that, after all the recent legislation upon trades
unions, the law should still remain id this un-
certain state; and it was agreed that the working
classes throughout the country rhould, be called

WORKERS.

There was held on Monday at Wolverhampton

Parker, chairman of the Ironmasters' Association,
was the president, and each side was represented
by 12 masters and men respectively.
The operatives explained that after holding
meetings in all the districts, and thereby ascertain-
ing the views of the men, they desired that the
masters would allow the wages of the next six
months to be based upon the prices of bar iron in
the past six months, and one shilling bonus. This,
they maintained, was the spirit of their agreement
and they urged that the published reports
proved it.
The masters offered to continue to pay 12s. 6d.
a ton for three or six months, and at the and of
two or five months to discuss any terms for a
future settlement. They contended that the iron-
workers, by joining those in the North of England
and elsewhere, had changed the basis of the former
agreement, which they had also. broken.
The men denied that anyone in any other dif-
trict had suggested the course they should take.
They then asked that the difference should be sub-
mitted to arbitration. .

The masters decline arbitration for the North
of England. The men did not observe the arbi.
trators' award when wages was last raised
here.

The men asked the masters to advance upon
12s. ed. if iron rose. The qUestion involved the
inquiry, would the men accept a reduction if prices
dropped? They could pledge the rest of the trade
to the terms.they had offered; those terms were
the masters' it!timatum, and on them the works
would be thrown open. The men expressed dis-
appointment, and will hold an aggregate meeting.

, The increasing interest - taken in. Canada of
late years and
.the steady flow of immigration,

But the query, ‘,‘ What is Ontario ?" is still, to a

problem. The precise limits of the province are,.

With this view ten agents (or ;commissioners)

CHRISTMAS.

ALTIIOITGII Christmas is kept on the twenty-
fifth of December, the learned in such matters
remain unable to determine with general con-
sent the birthday of the Incarnate CIIRIST.
If we may still accept the authority of Sir
ISAAC NEWTON as not yet superseded by more
recent ehronologers, the assignment of that
event to this season of the year was due to the
tendency of the older men of science to make
Christian dates coincident with cardinal points
of the year; religious leaders, so long is a
fixed time of commemoration was appointed,
being quite content. "The times of the birth
and crucifixion of Our SA.vrouu," it is observed
by one who, as a matter of learned inquiry,
had taken great pains to make himself master
of the subject, "are so written in the Gospels
that nothing certain can be determined con-
cerning them; and all who have pretended to
settle these periods are conjoeturers, and not
historians, as their variety proves. There are
more than one hundred and thirty opinions
concerning the year of His Nativity; and the
day of it has been placed by men of equal
learning in every month of the year. Let us
respect the silence of the oracles of GOD. A.
point of chronology is not an obj cot of saving
faith ; nor is zeal for an undecided question
any part of that holiness without which none
shall see the Loup. The inspired writers did
not design to make laws about feasts, but to
enforce the practice of piety and virtue."
In these sentences, we have the fundamental
reason that nearly all classes of Protestant
Dissenters from the Established Church,
decline to follow her example in the feasts and
the fasts which she orders to be observed.
From her eves, vigils, and saints' days gone-
rally Ahoy turn awayw ith mere than indiffere nee,
and treat thew, at tha mildest, with almolute

neglect. But, in all likelihood, most of them
would have gladly made a distinction in favour
of events so. vital to the Christian faith us the
birth and the death of Orritm, could those sub-
lime anniversaries have been ascertained by a
successful chronology. Their readiness to ac-
cept what might be so verified, is shown in the
nearly unanimous adoption of the first day of
the week as the Lou's Day of the Universal
Church. The crucifixion of JESUS on Friday
and his resurrection on Sunday, are facts as
clearly revealed and precisely- determined.by
the evangelical records; as, by the same
documents, the particular days, whether of
birth, death, or rising again, are left altogether
indeterminate.

•' There can be liitle doubt, moreover, that
many really religious Men, induced in the first
instance, to ignore the observances in question
on historical grounds, were confirmed in their
habit,- and have been, sustained on the past of
similar men in subsequent generations, by the
moral antipathy to careless, violent, or ex-
aggerated assumption of a religious spirit
upon a few days of the year, an 3. still More by
the manner rin which the so-called "feasts of
the Church" were allOsved to degenerate from
holy days, in form at least, into days of
rough
.revel and loose license. In this re-
spect, however; Christmas-day has, atriong
ourselves, recovered the respectability, of its
character as a aisy of cessation from business,
if not also as one of ceremonious 'religious
observance. The "Lord of Misrule" has
entirely disappeared ; and even " the wassail
bowl," not merely as ancisntly replenished and
sent 'round, but in the modern substitute of
cups which both cheered and inebriated wait-
ing upon each, has *rapidly come to be re-
garded as a thing. more honoured in the
breach than in the observance. The manner
in which . Christmas•day is now kept—the
manner in Which it was . enjoyed on Wedness.
day last, for instance—holds a happy mediuM
between the two extremes of custom which ever
distinguished it, doe's not affect a high tone of
ecclesiastical authority and religious reverence
on the one hand, now, on the other, in point
of convivial festivity, either contravene the
essential spirit of genuine Christianity or
transgress the limits of a serious moderation.
If, for example, the stipendiary magistsate
did not all on Thursday morning make
reference to the fewness, of the' cases of
excess in drink, and consequent disorder,
brought hope then, it was probably because
that which some years ago was a beneficial
change too palpable to pass unnoticed, is now
happily become
,too little the exception and too
much the rule to call forth the comments of
agreeable surprise.
From the highest to the humblest, from
court to cottage, from queen to guarder, all
England was on Wednesday divided into
family parties, in many instances re-united
from distant places, and oven different quar-
ters of the globe. What pictures could be
more pleasing to GOD or
,to man? Is it
possible that the nativity of the MBE of
BETULEIIEU could be celebrated in any way
more pleasing to Him who loved to sit down
with the Family of Betb.any, and whose last,
act upon the Cross was to provide a new home
for the heart-wrung Mother who saw Him
writhing upon the cursed tree? . The Divine
Apostle of Peace and Goodwill can see nothing
that more compensates His cruel sufferings
for the sake of universal man than the cul-
tivation of family ties and the cheerful dis-
charge of neighbourly kindnesses. These,
it must be acknowledged, are now the groat
features of an English Christmas; and nothing
'can be conceived of as better adapted to unite
,the nation by indissoluble links, and make it
'pulsate with kindly feelings as though it had
but one heart. Under this aspect even joys
might join with Christian in the annual
festival. Ton thousand dinner-tables on Wed-
nesday last, and ten times ten thousand in-
dividual benefactions on Wednesday next, may
justly be considered as embodiments of JESUS'S
direction, "When thou !naked a feast, call
the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind,
and thou halt :be be blessed, for they cannot
recompense thee, for thou shalt be recom-
pensed at the resurrection of the just ;" and ;
of that other title to his highest consideration !
at Us° final judgment, "Inasmuch as yo

have done it -unto-one-of the least of those
my brethren,,Ye haVe'dono it unto Me;" and
in what other ,respect did this Jew of Jew%
more magnify and make honourable the law-
of His Divine Father. and Human Ancestry,'
hat blessed law, according to whose fraternal
Custom NEITEKLUT, the Governor, and Emu.
the. Priest, said to ail' the people, "ao your
way; eat the fat, and, drink- the. sweet; and
send portions to them for whom nothing is
prepared ;" while MoRDE&A in .eammemora.-

ESTHER, instructed them to make the four.'
teeuth and fifteenth days of the month of Mar
"days of feasting and joy, and of sending por-
tions one to another, and gifts to the poor."

THE .SENTENCE ON THE OAS STOKERS.
Tim relentless
,:ninuer in which the Gas
Companies have pursued their stokers, , and
the severity of the sentences passed on them,
are matters of the deepest significance to all
workmen. We see that in spite
.of all the
talk we have had about "freedom of contract"
find the like, there are plenty of persons who
still cherish intense hatred of ull concerted
action by workmen—the only way of securing
this. And we see that so soon as the public
temper' will tolerate it, laws framed to suit'
totally differept social state, and new practi-
cally obsolete, will be enforced with the ut-
most harslines&

That an act of gross injustice has been done.
public opinion will in no long time icortainly
pronounce. Five men have bean punished'
with twelve months' imprisonment (us unable

!writer puts it) for injuring the London Gas
Light Company "by combing to force it 'to
change its mode of business." And the. Bello
tells us that " the, stokers have been punished
as heavily as persons found guilty of man
slaughter and putting stones on a line with a
view to upset a railway train, and at least.
twice as severely as, a man who had incited a
bull dog to worry his wife." There can bone
doubt that the threatened • ineenvenience 'and
danger to the publi i at the bottom of the
irritation.of public feeling. We would not, for.
amoment, justify the strike.. But too much has
been made of it,. It has been assumed through-
outthat it was impossible for the directors to
give way out of consideration . for the .public
safety. One would think that the will of those
gentlemen is a law of nature against ,which it,
is both absurd , and wicked to fight. It was
not the obstinacy of ,one, but the obstinacy of
both parties that caused the danger.to London.
The main question now is, What is to be
done ? We must avoid wasting, energy in
abusing Mr. Justice Burn, though his conduct
both in refusing to allow time for the prepara-.
tion of the defence, and in inflioting so heavy
a punishment, despite the jury's strong re-
commendation ,to mercy, is. fair subject for
comment. But our chief business is, first, to
see that the men's wives and children are pro-
vided for ; second,.' to bring pressure to bear on
the Government by deputations and memo-
rials to Mr. GLAnsToNu and Mr. BRUCE;
third, to have the law altered so that such in-
justice cannot occur again. The first of these
matters the Union will probably prefer to
attend to themselves, but, if necessary, a
public subscription for the purpose would meet
with abundant support. Mr. BRUCE finds no
diffloultyin reprieving persons guilty of pecu-
liarly atrocious murders. We may hope that
with sufficiently strong representations he
may be made to see that to counsel a strike is
not quite twice as wicked 49 to keep a bulldog
worrying one's wife for an hour-and-a,half,
and that there is here a fitting ease for the
exercise of the royal prerogative. ,

But the alteration of the law is the most
important of all, and this it is which will cost
most effort., to obtain. Many thousands of
men and women are now smarting as if under
a personal wrong, and Air a time England will
be made to ring. What we must guard against
is danger that the zeal of many will wax cold.
The feeling must be kept alive. The indigna-
tion must only give place to a settled determi-
nation for repeal. It must never be forgotten
that not the application, but the existence of
the law, constitutes the injustice of the ease.
There is no question here of Conservative or
Liberal. Some of us suspect that where Fr-
sonal rights are concerned there is little to
choose between parties. It is itot

question of union and non-union workmen.
Workmen of all shades of political opinion can
well afford to bury their differences and unite
for a time on this, Whatever members of
Parlianient.value or despise, there is one thing
they value, and that is their seats. And when
they perceive that the matter is not a nine
days' wonder, but that electors mean mischief,
they will shortly yield to a demand they dare
not refuse. A. few years since workmen were
in a very different position—were, in fact,
nearly as badly off as women householders are
now. The only Way would then have been to
persuade or frighten lthe fortunate possessors
of power into taking up our cause. We have
changed all that. Under household snifrage
and the Ballot, workmen can now compel Par-
liament to do them justice. They;have never yet
realized their own fitrength ; this may be ex-
pected to teach it them. Power they have in
plenty. If through disunion, through apathy'
or through want of persistence they fail to
exact justice, they are unworthy of the tradi-
tions of their class and must continue to suffer
an injustice for which they may then thank
themselves.

DIRECT REPRESENTATION OF LABOUR
AND ELECTION EXPENSES.
TILE question of the reduction and, transfer-
ence of election expenses is one of the greatest ,
importance as affecting the interests of labour,
and, until Parliamentary candidates can be
relieved from them it will be very difficult
always to secure the election of. working men.
In the old days of Parliamentary strugglea•
there were large prizes to be fought for.
Government influence meant family influence,
and family influence with party politicians
meant family gain. The great leading families
fought for the Parliamentary party to which
they belonged, and spent large sums of money
in the various conflicts that arose; but they
were paid back again by posts and promotions
in the public service, by pensions, and sine-
cures, and titles, and all else desirable as pro-
perty or influence that could. be conferred or
enjoyed at the expense of the nation.
. These old. contests were only open to rich
men. Voters, restricted in numbers as tbey
wore, were merely the tools of the chief actors,
and when we add the restriction imposed by
a heavy property qualification it will be easily
understood that the making of the nation's,
law, and the shaping of the nation's destiny
were meant only to be in the hands of the
powerful and the rich.
In the true aeoeptation of the word, the
"people" were scarcely considered at all, and
their interests and happiness had -only such
thought as was requisite to make them—and.
keep them—as a great balancing power, used
for the purpose of steadying and upholding
the party in office, or "sfor helping those not in
to got there.
We heed not insist here that this heavy
money expenditure at elections prevented con-
stituencies looking for any but rich candidates.
This was made quite clear by the fact that
the abolition of the property qualifloation did
not bring poor men into the field, The richest
men remained still all powerful, because by
the corrupt maohincrrir• in use, worked by all
sorts of clever and unscrupulous agents, and
by aid of money, lavisbly spent, the large
purse carried the day against the slender
one.

We need not enumerate the dishonest shifts
by which these parties attained their ends.
We 811 know they did attain them, and we all
know, in addition, that our Parliament is not
composed of England's " wisest and best," but
rather of England's richest men, anxious in
Many oases to promote special interests—in
many cases deftirous to attract public notice by
their position—and it would be wrong to omit
the statement• that, at least in the legal pro-
fession, there are some who regard a seat in
the Rouse of Commons as a bench from which
to climb to prefessional honour and emolu-
ment.

The Ballot Bill, as introduced into the House
by Mr. FORSTER, was the first Governmental
proposal to give the working classes a chance
with others to enter the House of commons.
The clause in that Bill to remove the expenses
from the shoulders of the candidates was a
great stop in advance. This, if passed into
Jaw, would really have opened the door for

the representatives of labour. Men who had
friends n a constituency, and who were known
as well-informed and fit persons, by a slight
outlay for placards and other personal ex-
penses might, had that clause been carried;
have been sent into the House of Commons, to
represent the cause of labour, not necessarily
in a class spirit, but simply as putting labour
on the same level as all other national in-
terests.

The working men, and men of intelligence,
and tried charaoter, but of slender means,
qualified to represent them, really did look
with hope to this provision of the Ballot
Bill. Bat it is to be feared that
.00rtain
members of the Liberal party regarded it
with great dislike, and by their conduct suc-
ceeded in removing it from the Bill, and
with the help of those who hate the liberaliz-
ing of our institutions, have left working men
in their old position of exclusion, helpless
almost in themselves, and trusting to others
for that Careful and :Wise protection of their
interests which cannot be obtained from Per-
sons, however well intended, who are not of.
their own order, and directly in connection.
with them. • '

Now, the question naturally arises here,
as to how working men should deal with the
persons who on this occasion were most pro-
minently mischievous in relation to this matter
of election expenses? Shall they listen to the
old cry—" Oh, don't divide the party," or shall
they treat them as having sinned against the
whole Liberal creed, and punish them. as
political offenders in the worst sense of the
word? . With
,working men this question of
election expenses is a vital one. It means
absolute ox-clusion from the House of Com-
mons, It means a continuance of political
degradation.. It means the abandonment of
the working man's chief interest to the hands
of persens not equal to its adequate protection.
It
.is all very well to say that these persons
belong to the Liberal party ; still, the work-
ing men can only regard them with dis-
trust, and instead of our operatives—under any
sense of allegiance being asked to vote for
them, they should be thrown over and dis-
carded by the leaders of the Liberal party,
that sound policies may. be' pursued and
discipline secured by the severe punishment
,of conspicuous traitors. Mr. LIENEY JAMES,
the member for Taunton, cannot, in this
, matter, be forgiven by any working man who
respects himself, or who is interested in the
welfare of his class, and never again under
any plea of general liberality ought he to be.
accepted as a true friend of the working
people. He may be very
.anxious to servo
working men by his advocacy and his votes,
but we are very much mistaken if working men
would not 'prefer to take the guardianship of
their own interests into their own hands to
leaving them to the protection of aspiring
lers, Who, as a rule, give their chief care
to their own advancement, and- who may be
anxious to help others when by so doing they
are quite satisfied they'can help themselves.
If the Working men are called on to give
their support to any political party, the
questions which lie nearest their own hearts
should form a portion of the programme of'
that party, abetrayal of these questions should
absolutely disqualify for Parliamentary
honours those guilty of such betrayal, and the
party cannot, do better than begin by dealing
with such offenders as we have:pointed out.
That working men must go into Parliament
should be 'the conclusion of every Liberal
mind, and as a necessary first step pretended
friends, who arc really 'their worst enemies,
should be driven out to make room for them.
Wo must, in fact, cease to play with serious
questions, and consolidate the great Liberal
party by insisting on horiesty and earnestness
in its leading Members.

ACTION AGAINST THE AIIiALGAAIATED

IT may not be out of place to say a word or
two on a ease brought before the Judge of the
County Court at lieweastle•on-Tyno a few
days since. A man named YOUNG was the
plaintiff; and WILLTAAE Amix-N, General
Secretary of the Amalgamated Engineers, de-
fendant.

You°, having arrived at the age of fifty, and
having subscribed for 21 years to the fluids of

Under these circumstances YOUNG brought

less than in any other ought such mischievous

subordination to such mutual compacts, that
any good common to all can be effected. The
Amalgamated Engineers pay 4.10,000 a year

run the risk of dissipating one shilling of such
a fund in miserable legal squabbles is an al-
most unpardonable folly. Trade societies
should rely implicitly on their arbitration
clauses. Their members should understand

who, in nine cases out of ten, would much
rather see them all gd to wreck than not;
especially if they could get profit or reputation
thereby.

AMONGST the speech- making of the last few
days two very remarkable addresses have been
delivered, one by Mr. GLA,DSTONE to the
pupils of the Liverpool College, the other by
the Niko of SOMERSET at the Newton Abbot
Art and Science Schools.

Mr. GLIDSIONE'S address had in it many
very fine passages, but what must strike the
reader as remarkable was the gloomy, almost
cowardly view taken by the hon.gentleman, in
relation to the action of modern free thought, or
rather as he styled it, the " extremest forms of
unbelief," as developed in the writings of
STaAuss and others. On such a subject there
can be no controversy here, but ought it not
strike every thinking man that in every age of
the world there has been extreme forms of
thoughts upon all subjects, and that punish-
ing them, or warning people against 'them,
never yet did good to anybody. On the con-
trary, has it not always been found that such
punishments and cautions have frequently led
to immeasurable evils.

The worst days of perseoution have passed,
with all their detestable horrors, and we are
all pleased that such is the ease. We now
give the utmost latitude to thought on all
subjects of human investigation, and this right
will be jealously guarded by all liberal men.,
Its exercise will, no doubt, lead to error.
Neither scientifie nor critical investigations
are all successful in the pursuit of truth.
Every duty has its danger, and the time
ought to have gone by with us when
cautions are needed in regard to honest in-
vestigation, especially when we remember
that We consider the truth we hold as a people
on the most sacred subjects, is considered by
its as the truest and loftiest that can be held
by man.
Mr. GnenSTONT, no doubt, meant well, but
can it be doubted that he did more harm than
good. in giving to an "immense audience" a
caution much more calculated to awaken
curiosity than to fortify faith. The cowardli-
ness of • intelleot thus exhibited always leads
to its own punishment. The caution in this
instance will, no doubt, lead to a perusal of
the condemned works, and as in the books the
arguments in favour of their leading ideas will
be found fully stated, they are certain to
have what Mr. GLIDSTONE believes to be an
undesirable effect, seeing that the young
reader will have little to oppose to them, but the
warning of which he has taken. no heed, and

which carries with it:no rebutting argument.
There was in England once a statesman who

thought, and his praise of science and scientific
