DEo. 28, 1872.

A. FRENCH WORKI&AN ON THE
. WORKING CLASSES.

_
BY GABRIEL MOLLIN, WORKING GILDER.

If we consider, on the one band, the numbers of
the working classes, the boldness of their views,
the warmth oftheir feelings, and the energy they
put forth, and, on the other hand, if we contem-
plate their social condition, we are at once struck
by the painful contrast between their worth and
usefulness to society and the rilative -position in
it which they at present occupy. In face of this
contrast, many speakers and writers have yielded
to an unworthy despair, and have drawn •conclu-
sierra of the most disheartening kind. It has even
been maintained that the workman had no im-
provement to hope for, that the injustice of which
he is the victim is a necessary evil, that the heavy
burden, which be alone carries till he is crushed
by it, is placed on his shOulders by a pitiless fate,
to remove which all human efforts arc powerless.

Fortunately, this is not true. If the workmen
have failed hitherto to better their lot, the reason
is that their efforts have been dir,ected by prin-
ciples which are either inadequate or positively
airs; they have tried many paths, which have
led them in all directions but the right.
The writer of these lines is one who has per-
sonally taken part in these divers efforts. He
knows the difficulties which surround the prepa-
ration fur them, and the bitter isolation caused by
clesettion in the hour of trial. Still he has never
doubted for a single moment of the ultimate
triumph of our cause. Experience has shown him
the inadequacy of the means hitherto employed,
but in no wise shaken his faith in the future.
Now, having followed cross-roads, which led not
to the desired goal, he enters the great highway.
Ile had been Mistaken; let us examine where his
mistake lay.
Every one admits that, in order to perform the
simplest operations a certain special knoiledge is
indispensable; that, in order to cast up a sum
in addition, we must know how to count; that no
man can follow a trade without having learnt it.
bus, to construct a building it is necessary to have
studied the particular nature of theground on which
it is to stand, and the materials must be arranged
conformably with a settled plan. If workmen wore
to undertake the Construction of an edifice, re:
gardlesa of thesa conditions, we should not hesitate
to call them fools. They might say what they
liked about their good intentions, that they worked
in the best spirit; we elmuld not believe one whit
the more in the success of their enterprise; for
we know that, with all the good-will in the world,
no one will ever make a piano, build a ship or a
house, without the special knowledge requisite
for these operations.
Well, then, the solution of social problems de-
mands similar qualifications, with this difference:
that the phenomena in question, being much more
complicated, require a much greater knowledge in
those who undertake them, and this requirement
has been overlooked. We had been led to think
that the workmen, by reason of their great num-
ber, the boldness of their projeots, the sincerity of
their intentions, and their fearless courage, could
make up for their want of knowledge. There was
our mistake. We had believed that, by yielding
to metaphysical illusions, we could do without the
support of science. It was an immense error. In
refusing to listen to serious thinkers, while we
gave a ready ear to the empty declamations of
metaphysicians, we were in the wrong, and have
covered Ourselves with ridicule; because meta-
physics, whieh sacrifice observation to imagination,
well-fitted as they are for the pursuit of idle di-
luents, are, for that very reason, unfitted for the
pursuit of real knowledge.
And indeed, the metaphysicians do not deem,
they imagine; instead of registering facts, they
invent them; instead of thought, they give us
dreams; and thus they have developed all their
philosophical absurdities on the existence of the
ego, of the "I," the equality of minds, and the
sovereignty of the majority, and have evolved
their endless social theories, which we have ac-
cepted on too easy terms.
Thus metaphysics are incapable of establishing
that general, mutual uuderstanding which is indis-
pensable to society. .And further, human dignity
requires that the relations which connect indi-
viduals and classes should be spontaneous and
voluntary, and not forced; accepted, and not im-
posed. Under these oonditions, the need of a doc-
trine purely scientific, embracing the same total of
all real knowledge, and the methods of which,
always susceptible of demonstration, indicate the
proper course to be followed in any given case,
will be, felt by all to be urgent. It will be ad-
mitted, raoreover, in agreetnent with the disciples
of Augusto Comte, that the worldly improvement
in the workman's position depends on his moral
and intellectual l'egeneratiou, and that the reorga-

nisation of opinions and morals ought to precede
and not follow the reform of institutions; and
that, consequently, at the present time theoretical
speculations are the most practical of all.
Thus the cart has been put before the horse, and
we have in consequence to deplore the loss of power
and the shipwreck of efforts, and buoyant hopes
dashed to the ground in the pumerous schemes
attempted up to the present time, with the design
of improving the condition of the workman. Well
then, fellow-toilers, if we wish seriously to parti-
cipate in a social reorganisation, of which we all
feel the imperative need, it is absolutely indis-
pensable that we should replace our vague desires
and our chimerical aspirations by clear aud firm
convictions, grounded on positive principles, such
as will determine the legitimacy of our pretensions
and the character of our duties, and throw a light
on the course which is before us.
Inasmuch as social questions can be resolved
neither by force nor law, their solution being pre-
eminently dependent on calm reasoning, requiring
order in the street and clearness in the head, we
have in the first place :-
1. Refolutely to lay aside all forms of' forcible
insurrection in the interests of our opinions.
2. To withhold our adhesion from those de-
claimers who pretend that our social amelioration
depends upon their political advancement.
3. To declare that the action of Government
must confine itself to the proteation of the liberty
of all.
Further, in conformity with the teaching of
social science, which takes real facts as the only
basis from which our action can start, and which
proves that the division of the industrious classes
into two categories, those of capitalists and.
labourers, is an inevitable result of anteceden
social forces, we arc bound to accept, as a fixed
point in social order,. the separation of the indus-
trial.army into employers and artizans, or, in other
words, into a patriciate and a proletairiate.
In saying this WO only express the deepest feel-
ings of the working class, which treats with pro-
found indifference all that is incapable of a real
and practical application. Are increase of know-
ledge and comfort, a lessening of fatigue and toil,
these seriously, guaranteed are at bottom all that
workmen really' wish for; the greater number
openly accept the present basis on which indus-
trial action reposes, stipulating energetically, let i
be well understoood, that it shall receive such
modifications as its nature admits. This position
will, no doubt, be disputed by the charlatans of
socialism, but we fear not to maintain it, supported
as it is by direct observation of fact.
We have to aim, therefore, at the abolition
neither of capitalists nor workmen; on the con-
trary, our object should he the establishment of
wholesome relations between these two classes.
Before discussing the respective functions of the
two elements which constitute moderti society, let
us first enquire into the nature of the capital
which it possesses. Auguste Comte divided
material wealth into two great groups—let, in-
struments or tools;' 2nd, provisions. The distinc-
tive mark of the objects which constitute the first
group consists in their having always a character
of public utility; land, raw material, instruments
of labour belong to it. The successful employ-
ment of this kind of capital depends on its con-
centration in the hands of the partricians, of the
chiefs of industry. The workmen, therefore, are
called upon gradually to renounce all claim to the
possession of this kind of wealth. Its administra-
tion devolves on the employers, whom we must,
for the future, consider as simply the holders of the
oapital of society, the production of successive
generations which they are called upon to utilize
in accordance with the rules of social morality.
Secondly. Food, clothing, lodging, &c., every-
thing having a personal use, constitute the second
group. The personal origin of the wants thus
satisfied necessitates a personal distribution of the
objects which compose it, that distribution which
extends itself to families must be effected by the
means of exchange, that is purchase and sale;
consequently the profits of the patricians and the
wages of the workmen ought to be proportionate
to the personal and domestic wants of both those
classes.
Let us now enquire into the four social func-
tions of the employers, viz., direction, distribution,
conservation, and transmission.
By direction we understand direct personal and
effective administration of the wealth owned by
every industrial chief.
By distribution, the share due to each co-
operator, that is to say his wage, which, let us not
forget, must be sufficient for the support of the
family.
By conservation we mean the keeping up, the
improvement, and the increase of the plant; and—
By transmission, the duty incumbent on the
capitalist to transmit to a successor the aggregate
of,oapital of which he has had the employments

The functions of the workman have been
classed as follows by M. Magnin, working car-
penter, President of the Positivist Society at
Paris

1. Regeneration. 2. Work. 3. Protection. 4.
Appreciation. •
The first function which the mass of workmen
has to discharge is the formation of a future race
of workers, which shall, at least, equal itself in
number, vigour, intelligence, and. morality: The
proper discharge of this function requires that the
wife shall be freed from • nil industrial labour in
order that she may devote herself entirely to her
mission of housekeeper and teacher.
The second function of the workmen is the
execution, under the guidance of the employers,
of all those industrial operations which the legiti-
mate needs of society demand. We say legitimate
needs, in opposition to arbitrary cravings, and we
advise workmen to protest energetically against
all action which subordinates the needs physical,
intellectual, and moral of their class to the lawless
caprices of certain idlers.
For the matter of that, the regenerated workman
will know well how to recall the decency that
pack of spendthrift's who, Under the pretext of
giving us work, madly squander the produce of
our labour. They will remind them that all ex-
penditure of power, which has for its object the
consolidation or the improvement of society, is
blameworthy; that every undertaking width does
not confer oil the human race security and well-
being commensurate with the toil it has cost is
one worthy of condemnation, aud they will refuse
peremptorily to participate in any enterprise in-
adequately authorized by public morality.
The third function arises from the fact that
there will always be a class of feeble persons whom
it is the duty of society to help. Hence the
necessity of a system of protection. Whatever that
systein, may be, its cost will always fall on the
worker, and, as M. Magnin says, will be the
heavier the less directly it is met. That is why,
as he adds, the workman should voluntarily under-
take the, direet -protection of the weak, the infirm,
and the sick, of such as can be left without danger
in families. The Workman, therefore, in the name
of the sacred principle of the family, should re-
pudiate and eondemn all those philanthropic and
Jesuitical institutions such as almshouses, public
nurseries, hospitals and asylums, as such barrack-
prisons ought in the future to afford a refuge to
those only whose diseases threaten a real danger
to health, security, or public morality.
The fourth function of the 'workman is to con-
stitute a public opinion whieh -consists in the
appreciative judgment of all the acts which com-
pose social existence.
The nature of these important functions demands'
for their discharge the application of the Positivist
theory of wages which we consider as the necessary
indemnity paid to the workmen in order that they
may , accomplish their antics as regenerators,
toilers, protectors, and appreciators. It is the sum
paid to the workman adequate to the satisfaction
of his physical needs and of those of his family; it
is in no sense an equivalent of the work furnished
by him, but a contribution destined to enable him
to work at all.

What is wanted, therefore, is a complete and
radical transformation in the motives which actuate
all ranks in the industrial army. lip to this time
their motives have been selfish and servile, their
views have not been those of the citizen and the
free man. Our capitalists acknowledge no obliga-
tions of a civic kind; generally their motives are
purely personal. Hunger for wealth, an im-
patience to make a fortune which will relieve them
of all duty, are the ruling impulses of their'
enterprisos.

As regards the workmen, their precarious con-
dition diminisheq, to a great extent, their responsi-
bility in the matter, but we cannot deny, indeed
we deplore, that they have fallen into such an
abject state that they have been induced to approve
of any amount of recklessness, and to take their
share in all enterprises, whatever they be; that by
sacrificing their personal duties, civic and domestic,
to a grasping industrialism, they have trodden
underfoot all that is most elevated in man.; that,
in a word, by lowering themselves for wages, even
to participating in operations which they condemn,
under the direction of people whom they despise,
they have (in thus imitating their superiors) pro-
stituted their activity, just as the street-walker
prostitutes her charms.
This degrading position, which afflicts workmen
and capitalists alike, is the origin of all our
industrial conflicts. These feuds between wealth
and numbers will only be avoided in prOportion as
capitalists and workmen assume an attitude worthy
of the dignity of their vocation, that is by waking
a truly social impulse the chief motive of their
notion, and looking on each other as mutual allies
aiming at a omen:ion end, while their ittuctlone
are &Aka,

It is only, therefore, by introducing the notion
of duty lute social relations, that the final organi-
zation of the human race will be achieved, and
that we shall rise to the dignity of citizens. This
is the problem before us to make of each man a .

true citizen, really incorporated into society, and
directly concerned in its prosperity, that is, to
make him a public functionary possessing a home,
and freely accomplishing the functions of, the
natural order to which he belongs.
The working class, as it at present exists, is not
effectively a part of society ; it does not consist, to
speak correctly, of citizens, inasmuch as they
do not own their own firesides, and their social
relations to other classes aro in no sense re-
gulated by common obligations accepted on both
sides. They really play the part in society of
machines which are used according to the caprices
and needs of the moment; the condition of these
mercenaries is the most painful that can be realized,
and it constitutes, moreover, a real social danger.
In order to leave no doubt as to what we menu,
let us suppose (and the supposition is already in
process of realization) that by the successive intro-
duction of scientific n; ethods into industry, one-
half of the existing workmen shall be sufficient to
execute the aggregate of the work required. It
will be seen that if the workman were incor-
porated into society such an event would be for
them an immense stop in the road of progress, as
its first result would be a diminution of their
labours.

But if their condition remain the same as it is
now, if the workmen reap no advantage from the
riches they create, such an event as we have sup-
posed, which would prevent the horrible spectacle
of extreme misery in the midst of abundance,
would be regarded by the workmen as the greatest
of calamities. They would curse all those who
have improved tools and machinery from Archi-
midos down to Vaucanson. Each of these illus-
trious men will appear to them as a genius of evil,
they will have nothing. but hatred for their
memory and contempt for their work. The most
hunger-smitten will sell their services for a morsel
of bread; the more impatient will break the in-
struments of work, and, in the meantime, the
large and terrible army of starvers will be getting
organized, will raise the standard of revenge, and
write upon it the despairing device of the Lyons
workmen---“ Let us live by work or die in battle."
Humanity will then witness the most awful contest,
the most fi ightful bloodshedding which ever stained
our globe, the war of extermination between the
full and tho empty..
This will be enough to show the great import-
mice of the social question. Its solution calls for
the co-operation of generous hearts and clear
intellects, of the friends of real order and the parti-
sans of effective progress.
. Just listen, 0 selfish Conservatives! Sworn
enemies of all progress 1 Disturbers of all order
The need is not, under the pretext of foreign wars
to sot the brother-worker of neighbouring nations
periodically cutting each other's throats in fratri-
cidal wars, nor to hire an army whose business it
is to keep in servitude the very persons who pro-
duce the things indispensable to the satisfaction of
your wants. On the contrary, the need is a rose-
lute attack on the question by making use of the
distinctive faculty of man, namely his reason, the
solo means by which the great modern problem
can be resolved, which, we cannot too often repeat
it, consists in the incorporation of working men
into society, in other terms, in banging about a
voluntary submission to reciprocal duties fitted to
regulate the relations of the workmen with the
other classes.

LOOKED OUT.

The snow was coming down fast—white, solid,
determined flakes, that seemed tJ have Come to,
stay all the •wi,for with us, and defied anything
to melt them 'away. They clung to the houses
that lined the streets until every projection and
lintel' looked as if it had been trimmed with
swan's-down by some eccentric architect. The
peaked roofs of the houses in the Side-streets were
heavy With the white load, and nodded to each
other with their snowy periwigs as if, suddenly
determined to cut modern fashions, they had gone
back to the powder of our ancestors, and were
congratulating themselves on the change.
There was snow on the sidewalks; deep, despe-
rate snow; treacherous, fair-faced snow, corerin,g
up all the thousand pitfalls and ruts of the great
city-streets, and burying all the filth and rotten-
ness of the town under one vast charitable mantle.
The few people that were , out :on foot floundered
along with quick laborious breaths,; unprotected
females were deep in it, and might be seen standing
in IMMO great drift looking damp and helpless.
Small boys dashed :through the huge banks like
water-dogs through. the white combs of the sea
surf. They plunged into it as if
,they had been
born Russians, and were continually taking snow.
baths. They seemed to love to get it into their
shoes, and hair, and...ears, and sometimes they
would emerge from a long dive under the surface,
skaking a perfect foam of flakes from their shaggy
coats.

A bitter wind began to drive the dry, thick
snow aslant. It buried its invisible nose in the
deep loose layers on the streets, and. rooted them
up into furrows like some wild howling animal.
It rushed round tho corners of the houses with a
sudden snap, as if it would garotte some passing
wayfayer, and then, as if mad with disappoint.
meat at not meeting a victim, go shrieking down
the street. '

It was a night to make Charity feel ill at ease.
A. night to make Charity, as she eat by her quiet
fireside, see desolate pictures in the coals, of poor
bouseless people shivering in rags in bleak corners
of the town. Pictures of tattered outcasts lying
°lose together in vain attempts to warm each
other with intertwined limbs that were as cold as
the snow itself ; and then the white flakes falling,
falling on the lethargic forms, until nothing could
be seen but a shapeless bump of snow, which,
when morning came, would give up its frozen
secret, and a newspaper paragraph headed "Found
Dead" would close the history.
The city soon became more silent. Late men
housed themselves in bar-rooms and corner public-
housoo, And drank defiance to the cold in steaming
tumblers of legal poison. Policemen, being mo-
rally convinced that it was a night for burglars
and garotters to be abroad, retired, according to
their eastern,. to the warm courts and corners, and
related stories of their past adventures with
a wisp house-breakers. The city Wow) silent,

and the snow, though falling as heavily as over,
came down noiselessly, as if it did not wish to
break the general peace.
- Just about this time, Unimpressed, I regret to
say, by the tranquillity of the neighbourhood, a
young gentleman was making a most abominable
disturbance in the strtet. He was standing on
the stoop Of an old-fashioned and rather decayed
looking mansion, kicking at the door with a pair
of boots that, as far as solidity was concerned,
seemed to be descended from thwe famous seven-
leagued boots familiar to my childhood. Kick !
kick! kick! A dull wooden thunder rumbled
through the dark street, and then h IMMO came,
as if the kicker was rather tired with his exer-'
tions. If there was any Recording Angel about,

night, he would, I fear, have had to make a

OUR MISCELLANY.

INDUSTRY ITS OWN REWARD.
Anything we make up our minds to do we can
do. There is nothing impossible to be done by de-
termined, persevering effort, and nothing of im-
portance can be accomplished without it. It was
labour that built the pyramids; by labour the arts
and science were brought to their present state of
perfection; and labour is necessary for the health
and happiness of all. Industry is the law of our
being, and wo are so -constituted that when the
law is fully recognized it brings its own regard.
Bodily labour is net the only kind Lira iS necessary
—mind and body should be exercised. In this way
.cheerfulness and iontenttnent are promoted, and
we are prepared to fill with honour any station as-
signed us by Providence. - We often- regard the
doom pronounced on man, "In the sweat of thy.
face shalt thou eat bread," a curse ; but it is
really a blessing, for we find that fill rational en-
joyment follows in the train of industrious labour,
whether physical or mental.

CHARACTER IS ESSENTIAL TO lIAPPI-

NESS.

Without a good ci;;;;-t-er happiness is never
known. All that exalts, ennobles, embellishes,
end dignifies humanity is blended in the beauty
and the glory of a truly genuine character.
All the treasures of ten thousand worlds will
not - compare in value .with one pure heart for
the production of all that is satisfying and blessed.
They will ,not purchase peace, Tor joy, nor
sacred rest, nor the sweet tranquillity of an un-
sullied conscience, nor one single moment's
real bliss. They can never be exchanged for
those golden-gloried virtues that blossom all over
a good character, like the blossoms on a thick
bed of relies, and which are as rich in the sweet
incense that the heart loves most as the flowers
are in refreshing fragrance.
The youth who places a porper estimate upon a
good character has learned a lesson that is more
valuable to him than anything else possibly
can be. He has learned the source of his purest
joys. .
But the happiness and blessedness of a good
character are not confined to the sunny chambers
of its possessor. Character is catching. If one
has a good character, he gives something of its
goadnes.s to all with whom he associates. If his
heart is radiant with the light of virtue, that
light gets out, and shines in upon the hearts of
others. He can scarcely look at another without
impressing some mark of his own character on the
heart of the one upon whom he gazes. A man's
face is almost always radiant with the light of his
true character. Character, like murder, will out.
It cannot long be concealed. You might as well
attempt to chain the lightning's in the black
caverns of the surface of the sun, as to lock up a
mans character, from the eight of his fellows. God
never designed that it should bo. Character was
made to he seen. It is the government of the
soul: put on, not only for the ceinfort and con-
venience of the wearer, but for the pleasure of
other people's eyes. It is not worn for self alone,
for that would be mean, but for all by whom it is
surrounded.

HOPE AND CHARITY.
An men to speak and to dream arti prone,

Of better 'days before them;
We see them striving and hastining on
To the happier goal that's o'er them.
The world's renewed as its strength decays,
But man hopes evcr for better days.
Thipo leads man into this earth below,
Round the boy d3th it brightly hover,
It lights up his youth with its magic glow,
Nor quits him when life is over:
When, aged and weary, his coon() must cease,
With "hope" on his tombstone, he slumbers in
peace.

It is not a fiction empty and vain,
From a fool's dull brain descended ;
A voice in our heart cries, once and again,
For better things we're.intended :
And the whispering voice can .hopes impart
That noter shall deceive the trusting heart.
A PROFITABLE USE OF TIME.
Make the most of time. Some have little leisure,
but there are sundry expedients, any one of which,
if fairly tried, would make that little leisure
longer. Most of the men who have died enormously
rich acquired their wealth not in -huge jndfll,
but by minute and, careful accumulations. It
was not one vast sum 'bequeathed to them after

another which overwhelmed them with inevitable
opulence; but it was the loose money which most
men would lavish away, the little sums which
many would not deem worth looking atter, the
pennies of which you would keep no reckoning—
these are the items which, year by year piled up,
have reared their pyramid of fortune. From these
money-makers let us learn the nobler " avarice tds
time." One .of the • longest and most elaborate
poems of recent times, was composed in the streets
by a physician in busy practice, during the brief
snatches of time when passing from one patient's
door to another.. And in order to achieve some
,good work which you have much at heart, you
may rot be able to secure an entire week, or own
an uninterrupted day. But try what you can make
of the broken fragments of time. Glean up its
golden dust—those raspings end parings of precious ,
duration, those leavings of days and remnants of
.hours which so many sweep out into the waste of
existence. And thus, if you be a miser of moments,
if you be frugal and hoard up odd Minutes and
half-hours and unexpected holidays, your care-
ful gleannigs may eke out a long and useful
life, and you may die at last richer in existence
than multitudes whose time is all their own.
The time which some men waste in superfluous
slumber and idle visits and desultory application,
were it all redeemed, would give
.them wealth of
leisure, and enabie them to execute Undertakings
for which they deem less worried life than theirs
essential. When a persons says, "I have no time
to improve my mind or to do a kind turn' to a
neighbour," be May be saying what he thinks, but
be should not think what ho says ; for if he. has
not got the time already, ho may. get it by redeem-
ing it: .

A carelessness of speech is a fertilo source of
estrangement in married people. Now, it is ton
inneh-. the fashion in all 'households to have a 'do'.
mesa° colloquy, very different in its tone and care-
fulness to that in use with strangers. Tho very
best of us, it is feared, are too prone to this; hut,
from wives to husbands, and the reverse, matri-
mony seems certainly to possess the chomical.pro-
perty of convertin7 sweets. into acids in no time.
Short answers—foe he direst of domestic happiness
—pr else no answers at all ; no conversation for his
leisure for whom, once on a time, lOU carefully
brushed up all your stores of knowledge; and an
utter obli von of the personal politeness which most
well-conducted people think due to a stranger;
Pity such things are kept, like your choicest pre-
serves and bonne.: botu*s' meetly for strangers.
None can piano too much value on domestic
warmth Of politeness, unmixed. of course, wiih
hypocrisy or shallow words. Kindness might be
a better word, perhaps, for what is meant; for
where there are kind hearts there is almost sure
to be a certain suavity of manner. But this
etiquette of the heart you keep, like your last
clothes, for company ; never thinking that every-
day uso is your true polish, not merely for the
baser metals, but oven to keep bright gold itself.
Regard those things in a higher light than as
mere everyday trifles; for home, domestie love,
joy, happiness—all bang on a series of well-
directed trifles, and small is her chance of happi-
ness who sees fit to neglect or overlook them en-
tirely.

THE FISH-WIVES OF. PARIS.
When Louis XVI. and Marie Antoinette were
led to the placo of execution, though at different
periods, the Parisian fish-women observed no
bounds to the exultation of their unhappy fate.
In their savage joy they danced before the cart
which led the royal captives along the street, made
mockery of their sufferings, and some held up
their clenched fists, exclaiming, that if there
were another world, they would bunt them out
even there and be revenged upon them.
When old General Custinelppeared Work, the
revolutionary tribunal, he was accompanied by his
daughter-in-law, Madame de Cuotine. She was
descending alone the steps of tho notable prison of
La Force, when a silent crowd, with, the most
infuriated gestures, gradually closed around her.
An exclamation, or the slightest token of fear,
would have been instantly fatal to her. She is
said to have bitten her lips until the blood cone, in
order to prevent herself from becoming pale. On

articles.text:
STANDING ORDERS.

1. The Congress shall consist only of delegates
representing bona fide Trades Societies, and
Trades Councils, and similar bodies, by whatever
name they may, for the time being, be called.
2. Each delegate shall come provided with a
credential signed by the officers of the society or
council he represents, certifying to his appoint-
ment, such credential to be given up to the Secre-
tary, immediately on his arrival at the Con-
gress.

3. The time of meeting shall be as follows 3-
on tho first day to assemble at 12 o'clock noon
prompt; on all other days at 9 30 a.m.'; adjourn
at 1, re-assemble at 2, and adjourn at 6 o'clock
each day.
4. The roll shall be called promptly to time
morning and afternoon, the names of all dele-
gates late or absent to be read over with the
minutes each morning.
6. At the opening of the annual Congress, the
Chairman of the Parliamentary Committee shell
take the chair pro forma until the Congress has
elected its own President.

6. A committee of three shall" be elected to
examine the credentials, and report thereon to the
meetnig.

7. The delegates shall then proceed to elect the
President of the Congress, preference being given
to a delegate Of the town where the Congress is
being held.

8. The Congress shall then elect a Secretary, a
like preference being given.
0. The Congress shall then elect a vice-Presi-
dent, a door-keeper and a messenger.
10. A standing committee of five shall then be
elected, to whom shall be remitted the whole
business of the Congress; the order of and subjects
for discussion, together with the whole financial
arrangements of the Congress. The vice-president
to be the chairman of the committee.
11. After the routine business of election of
officers and committee, the president shall formally
open the Congress with an address.
12. The standing committee, with a view to
securing a proper despatch of business, with perfect
fairness to all who have been to the trouble to
prepare papers, of which due notice has been
given, shall have power to divide the Congress
into sections, so that those specially interested in
any particular question may have the fullest
opportunity for its discussion.
13. The standing committee shall be allowed to
retire at 4 o'clock each day (one hour before
closing the sittings of Congress), for the purpose
of selecting and arranging the next day's pro-
gramme.
14. Each delegate shall pay to the treasurer, on
the first day of his arrival, the sum of 10a. towards
the expenses of the Congress; and in case he
represents more than one society, 10s. for every

ginal proposition, shall he put to the vote until
the first amendment is disposed of.

division.

the movers of the resolution and amendments, for
the purpose of trying to secure unanimity, by
blending the amendments in such a manner as will
be most conducive to the harmony of Congress
and the despatch of business.
20. No delegate shall be allowed to read a
second paper until after all other papers, of which
notice has been previously given, have been read,
unless by special permission and sanction of the
standing committee, and the formal consent of
Congress.
